beats.narration: Everything you build with Claude travels the same road: a web request to the Claude API. But there are four request patterns, for four different situations. Pick the wrong one, and you either leave users staring at a blank screen, or pay real-time prices for overnight work.

elements.text: wrong pattern = blank screens, or overpaying

beats.narration: At its core, Claude is reached over a REST API. Your code sends a request to an endpoint, with your API key and a JSON body, and reads a JSON response back. You can call that endpoint directly with any HTTP client. More commonly, you use an official SDK. Python, TypeScript, and others. The SDK is a thin convenience layer over the same REST API: it handles authentication, request construction, retries, and response parsing, so you write less boilerplate. Same API, same models, either way. The SDK just saves you from assembling requests by hand.

elements.text: the SDK: a thin layer on the same API

beats.narration: Now, how does the response come back? A synchronous request is the simplest pattern: send the request, wait, and the complete response arrives in one piece. That's fine for short responses, and for backend jobs where nobody is watching. But when a response is long and a user is watching, waiting feels broken. Streaming fixes that: the response arrives in pieces as the model generates it, over the same connection, using server-sent events. Output appears immediately, and your code reassembles the pieces into the final message. The rule of thumb: someone watching? Stream it.

elements.text: fine for: short answers, backend jobs

beats.narration: For high-volume work there are two patterns, and they solve different problems. First: concurrency. The Python SDK ships an async client that uses non-blocking async and await, so your application keeps working while requests are in flight. In TypeScript you don't need a separate client. The standard one is already promise-based. Second: bulk. The Message Batches API is for offline workloads: you submit a large set of requests in one call, get back an identifier, and poll for completion. Batch jobs can take up to twenty-four hours, and in exchange they run at a lower per-token cost. Perfect for offline pipelines, evaluation runs, and anywhere cost matters more than turnaround.

elements.code:
client = AsyncAnthropic()
await client.messages.create(...)
# app keeps working meanwhile

elements.text: TypeScript: standard client is already async
up to 24h · lower cost per token

beats.narration: So ask one question: is anyone waiting? Short answer and nobody staring: synchronous. A user watching: stream. Many requests in flight at once: the async client. Thousands of requests overnight, where cost wins: batch. That's the whole map. You've now got all four foundations. Next: the module wrap-up.
